findings.scenario: Two whole mktemp assignments to the same variable followed by a correct rm trap are accepted; the dictionary retains only the final binding, so the first root leaks. All 14 new leaky executable fixtures were accepted and exited 0. Thirteen left their sandbox TMPDIR nonempty; one unset TMPDIR after helper initialization and leaked in the default temporary directory. The complete gate also returned 0 with the reused-variable script in a tracked path. Other accepted leaks cover cleared bindings, unreachable traps or init, exit/return before rm, redefined cleanup functions, builtin trap overrides, helper name-only print traps, Bash function definitions without parentheses and heredoc text mistaken for executed code.
findings.action: Enforce the claimed restricted grammar, effective control flow and lifetime of each allocation, variable and cleanup handler, or use execution-based leak evidence for accepted scripts. Reject unsupported syntax instead of recognizing isolated lines as proof. Include all reproduced cases and require the full-gate reused-binding control to fail.

findings.requirement: R1: cleanup on failure, INT and TERM, including restricted entries
findings.scenario: The hygiene gate intentionally leaves 0000/0400 entries while running the old-helper permission control, but its own EXIT trap still restores only u+w. Delivering INT or TERM immediately before the permission-control repair leaves the sandbox in the caller TMPDIR and prints rm Permission denied. Both signal probes run the unchanged current gate; an external DEBUG hook only chooses the signal timing. Reverting the real helper chmod correctly makes the gate fail with exit 1, but also leaves its sandbox for the same reason.
findings.action: Make the hygiene script own and remove its entire sandbox on failed checks and handled interruptions, restoring traversal as the corrected helper does. Add negative-path and INT/TERM probes of the hygiene command itself and require its caller TMPDIR to be empty.
